Potter CJ.lab_name: Potter Lab, Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Potter CJ.role: As a PhD student with Tian Xu at Yale, showed in Drosophila that Akt directly phosphorylates Tsc2 and breaks up the Tsc1-Tsc2 complex, one of several 2002 papers that connected insulin-Akt signalling to TSC. He now studies insect olfaction
Potter CJ.sub: Professor of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine · postdoc with Liqun Luo, Stanford (2002–2010) · PhD in Genetics with Tian Xu, Yale (1996–2002)
story: Christopher Potter did his PhD in Tian Xu's lab at Yale. In the Atlas study he was first author on work in fruit flies showing that Akt phosphorylates Drosophila Tsc2 at two conserved sites, that Tsc2 lacking these sites no longer responds to Akt, and that such a mutant blocks Akt-driven cell growth (POT2002). Other groups reported the same Akt-to-TSC2 link in mammalian cells in the same year.

After a postdoc with Liqun Luo at Stanford, where he moved into neuroscience, Potter set up his own lab at Johns Hopkins. His group builds genetic tools to study how the insect brain detects and responds to odours, in Drosophila and in the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae.

highlights.POT2002: First author: showed in Drosophila that Akt phosphorylates Tsc2 at Ser924 and Thr1518 and that a Tsc2 mutant lacking these sites blocks Akt-driven growth.

Xu T.role: Drosophila geneticist whose Yale lab helped show that Akt controls growth by phosphorylating the tumour suppressor Tsc2, linking the insulin pathway to TSC
Xu T.sub: Chair Professor of Genetics and Vice President, Westlake University (since 2018) · Professor of Genetics, Yale University (1993–2018) and HHMI Investigator (1997–2018) · postdoc, UC Berkeley (1990–1993) · PhD, Yale (1990)
story: Tian Xu was the senior author of the Atlas study in which his Yale group showed, in fruit flies, that Akt directly phosphorylates Tsc2, disrupts the Tsc1-Tsc2 complex and needs these phosphorylation sites to drive cell growth (POT2002). This was one of several 2002 papers, alongside mammalian cell work from other labs, that placed TSC2 downstream of Akt.

Xu studied at Fudan University, earned his PhD at Yale and did postdoctoral work at UC Berkeley. He then spent 25 years on the Yale genetics faculty, where he was also a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator, before moving to Westlake University in Hangzhou in 2018 as Chair Professor of Genetics and Vice President.

highlights.POT2002: Senior author: fly genetics and biochemistry showing that Akt phosphorylates Tsc2 and that this is needed for Akt-driven growth.

Pan D.lab_name: Pan Lab, Department of Physiology, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas, Texas, USA)
Pan D.role: Fly geneticist best known for work on the Hippo organ-size pathway. In 2002 his group reported that the Tsc1 and Tsc2 tumour suppressors act upstream of TOR to restrain S6K activity, in flies and mammalian cells
Pan D.sub: Chair, Department of Physiology, UT Southwestern Medical Center, and HHMI Investigator · Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (2004–2016) · postdoc with Gerald Rubin, UC Berkeley (1993–1998) · PhD with Albert Courey, UCLA · member, National Academy of Sciences (2023)
story: Duojia Pan was the senior author of the Atlas study showing that Tsc1 and Tsc2 can bind TOR and act upstream of it in fly genetic tests, and that cells lacking Tsc1 or Tsc2 keep S6K active even when amino acids are withdrawn (GAO2002). The amino-acid part of this model was later revised, as amino acid sensing was traced mainly to the Rag GTPases, but the placement of TSC upstream of TOR held.

Pan studied biochemistry at Peking University, earned his PhD at UCLA with Albert Courey and did postdoctoral work with Gerald Rubin at UC Berkeley. He started his lab at UT Southwestern in 1998, moved to Johns Hopkins in 2004 and returned to UT Southwestern in 2016 as chair of Physiology. His lab is widely known for its work on the Hippo signalling pathway that controls organ size.

highlights.GAO2002: Senior author: showed in Drosophila and mammalian cells that Tsc1-Tsc2 act upstream of TOR and that their loss keeps S6K active under amino acid starvation.

Dennis PB.lab_name: Materials and Manufacturing Directorate, Air Force Research Laboratory, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base (Dayton, Ohio, USA)
Dennis PB.role: As a postdoc in George Thomas's lab at the Friedrich Miescher Institute, was first author on the 2001 study proposing that mTOR responds to cellular ATP levels independently of amino acids
Dennis PB.sub: Research biochemist, Air Force Research Laboratory (protein-based biomaterials) · postdoc with George Thomas, Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel (1993–2001) · PhD, University of North Texas (1993)
story: Patrick Dennis was first author of the Atlas study reporting that lowering intracellular ATP reduces signalling through the mTOR pathway even when amino acids are present, and proposing that mTOR itself acts as an ATP sensor (DEN2001). Later work showed that much of the energy signal reaches mTORC1 through AMPK and TSC2, so the direct ATP-sensor idea became one part of a larger picture.

Dennis earned his PhD at the University of North Texas working on human protein kinases, then spent eight years in George Thomas's group at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel studying how signalling controls protein synthesis. He later moved to the Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, where he works on protein-based biomaterials.

highlights.DEN2001: First author: showed that lowering ATP reduces mTOR pathway signalling independently of amino acids and proposed mTOR as an ATP sensor.

Montagne J.lab_name: CNRS, Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon, ENS de Lyon (Lyon, France)
Montagne J.role: Drosophila geneticist who, working in George Thomas's group, showed that flies lacking S6 kinase are small because their cells are small, not fewer, and helped characterise fly TOR
Montagne J.sub: CNRS researcher; 2026 affiliation Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon · previously led the team “Growth, metabolism and physiology in Drosophila” at I2BC (CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay), Gif-sur-Yvette · earlier Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel, in George Thomas's group
story: Jacques Montagne was first author of the Atlas study in which flies lacking the S6 kinase gene developed slowly and ended up much smaller, because their cells were smaller rather than fewer (MON1999). He was also a co-author of the characterisation of dTOR, the fly TOR gene, which showed that dTOR controls growth through dS6K (OLD2000). Both studies came from a collaboration between George Thomas's group at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel and Ernst Hafen's group in Zurich.

Montagne later moved to the CNRS in Gif-sur-Yvette, where he led a Drosophila group at the Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC) working on how S6K, nutrients and lipid metabolism control growth and physiology. His most recent publication lists the Institut de Génomique Fonctionnelle de Lyon.

highlights.MON1999: First author: showed that Drosophila lacking dS6K are smaller because of smaller cells, not fewer cells.
highlights.OLD2000: Co-author: helped characterise dTOR and its control of growth through dS6K in Drosophila.

Neufeld TP.lab_name: Neufeld Lab, Department of Genetics, Cell Biology and Development, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Neufeld TP.role: Uses Drosophila to study how TOR signalling controls cell growth and autophagy; his group was one of two that described the fly TOR gene in 2000
Neufeld TP.sub: Professor, Department of Genetics, Cell Biology and Development, University of Minnesota
story: Thomas Neufeld was the senior and corresponding author of the Atlas study showing that fly TOR (dTOR) is needed inside each cell for normal growth and for the extra growth driven by PI3K, and that extra S6 kinase can rescue dTOR mutant flies (ZHA2000). The work was a collaboration with researchers at Chiron Corporation and appeared in the same journal issue as a parallel dTOR study from the Hafen and Thomas groups (OLD2000).

At the University of Minnesota his lab studies how nutrients and growth factors control cell growth through TOR, and how TOR regulates autophagy, the recycling of cell contents during starvation, using the fruit fly as a model.

highlights.ZHA2000: Senior author: showed that dTOR is needed cell-autonomously for growth in Drosophila larvae and that S6 kinase overexpression rescues dTOR mutants.

Corradetti MN.lab_name: Radiation Oncology, Providence Queen of the Valley Medical Center (Napa, California, USA)
Corradetti MN.role: As an MD-PhD student at the University of Michigan, was first author on the 2004 study linking the LKB1 tumour suppressor to TSC2 through AMPK. He is now a radiation oncologist
Corradetti MN.sub: Medical director of radiation oncology, Providence Queen of the Valley Medical Center, Napa · residency, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania · MD and PhD in Cell and Molecular Biology, University of Michigan · undergraduate, Harvard
story: Michael Corradetti was first author of the Atlas study, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at the University of Michigan Life Sciences Institute, showing that LKB1, the gene mutated in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, lowers S6K and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation through AMPK and TSC2 (COR2004). Together with a parallel study by Shaw and colleagues it tied energy stress, via LKB1 and AMPK, to the TSC2-mTOR axis.

Corradetti completed an MD and a PhD in Cell and Molecular Biology at Michigan, with doctoral work on inherited cancer syndromes, then trained in radiation oncology at the University of Pennsylvania. He has published on radiotherapy for lung cancer and now practises as a radiation oncologist in Napa, California.

highlights.COR2004: First author: showed in cultured cells that LKB1 inhibits mTOR outputs through AMPK and TSC2.

DeYoung MP.lab_name: Ellisen Lab, Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
DeYoung MP.role: As a research fellow in Leif Ellisen's lab, was first author on the 2008 study showing that hypoxia switches off mTORC1 through REDD1 releasing TSC2 from 14-3-3 proteins
DeYoung MP.sub: Scientist in oncology research and development at GSK · research fellow with Leif Ellisen, Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center & Harvard Medical School · PhD with Ram Narayanan, Florida Atlantic University
story: Phillip DeYoung was first author of the Atlas study showing how low oxygen turns mTORC1 off: REDD1 frees TSC2 from inhibitory 14-3-3 proteins so that TSC2 can act, and cells lacking REDD1 fail to switch mTORC1 off in hypoxia and grow into larger tumours in mice (DEY2008).

DeYoung earned his PhD at Florida Atlantic University with Ram Narayanan, working on bioinformatic discovery of cancer genes, then joined Leif Ellisen's lab at the MGH Cancer Center as a research fellow. He moved into drug discovery at GSK, where he has worked in oncology research and development.

highlights.DEY2008: First author: showed that hypoxia inhibits mTORC1 through REDD1-driven release of TSC2 from 14-3-3 proteins.

Ellisen LW.lab_name: Ellisen Lab, Mass General Cancer Center, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Ellisen LW.role: Physician-scientist whose lab studies REDD1, a stress-induced inhibitor of mTORC1, and showed how hypoxia uses REDD1 to release TSC2 from 14-3-3 proteins
Ellisen LW.sub: Professor of Medicine, Harvard Medical School · Clinician Investigator and physician in Hematology/Oncology, Massachusetts General Hospital · MD and PhD, Stanford University (1992)
story: Leif Ellisen was the senior author of the Atlas study showing that hypoxia switches off mTORC1 because REDD1 releases TSC2 from inhibitory 14-3-3 proteins, and that loss of REDD1 favours tumour growth in mice, with low REDD1 seen in a subset of human breast cancers (DEY2008).

Ellisen earned his MD and PhD at Stanford and leads a lab at the Mass General Cancer Center, where he is also a practising oncologist. His group studies tumour suppressor pathways, including p53-family proteins and REDD1, and how they shape cancer cell signalling and metabolism.

highlights.DEY2008: Senior author: showed that hypoxia inhibits mTORC1 through REDD1 and 14-3-3 release of TSC2, with tumour-suppressor effects in mice.

Jones RG.lab_name: Jones Lab, Department of Metabolism and Nutritional Programming, Van Andel Institute (Grand Rapids, Michigan, USA)
Jones RG.role: Studies how nutrient and energy sensing by AMPK and mTOR shapes cell metabolism, especially in T cells and cancer. As a postdoc with Craig Thompson he showed that AMPK triggers a p53-dependent glucose checkpoint in the cell cycle
Jones RG.sub: Chair and Professor, Department of Metabolism and Nutritional Programming, Van Andel Institute (since 2018) · Assistant then Associate Professor, Goodman Cancer Research Centre, McGill University · postdoc with Craig Thompson, University of Pennsylvania · PhD with Pamela Ohashi, University of Toronto
story: Russell Jones was first author of the Atlas study showing that proliferating cells stop at the G1/S boundary when glucose runs short, even with amino acids present and mTOR active, and that this arrest needs AMPK to phosphorylate p53 on serine 15 (JON2005). The checkpoint runs in parallel to mTOR rather than through it.

Jones earned his PhD in Medical Biophysics at the University of Toronto with Pamela Ohashi and did his postdoctoral work with Craig Thompson at the University of Pennsylvania. He then ran a lab at McGill University's Goodman Cancer Research Centre before moving to the Van Andel Institute in 2018, where he chairs the Department of Metabolism and Nutritional Programming.

highlights.JON2005: First author: showed that AMPK activates p53 to stop the cell cycle when glucose is scarce, independently of mTOR.

Thompson CB.lab_name: Thompson Lab, Cancer Biology & Genetics Program, Sloan Kettering Institute, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Thompson CB.role: Cancer biologist whose lab studies how growth signals control the uptake and use of nutrients; senior author of the study that described an AMPK- and p53-dependent glucose checkpoint in the cell cycle
Thompson CB.sub: Benno C. Schmidt Chair of Cancer Research, Memorial Sloan Kettering · President & CEO of MSK (2010–2022) · University of Pennsylvania, Abramson Family Cancer Research Institute (from 1999) · University of Chicago (from 1993) · University of Michigan & HHMI (from 1987) · MD, University of Pennsylvania (1977)
story: Craig Thompson is the senior author of JON2005, done in his lab at the University of Pennsylvania with Russell Jones as first author. The study described a checkpoint at the G1/S boundary that stops dividing cells when glucose runs short. The arrest was run by AMPK and needed AMPK to phosphorylate p53 on serine 15. It happened even though amino acids were present and mTOR stayed active, so in these cultured cells the glucose checkpoint worked alongside mTOR rather than through it.

Thompson trained as a physician (MD, University of Pennsylvania, 1977) and held faculty posts at the University of Michigan and the University of Chicago before returning to Penn in 1999 as scientific director of the Abramson Family Cancer Research Institute. His earlier work covered T-cell costimulation through CD28 and the Bcl-2 family protein Bcl-xL; his later work moved to cancer metabolism. He led Memorial Sloan Kettering as president and CEO from 2010 to September 2022 and still runs a lab in the Cancer Biology & Genetics Program of the Sloan Kettering Institute.

highlights.JON2005: Senior author: AMPK induces a p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest when glucose is low, even while mTOR stays active.

Alexander A.lab_name: Morgan Welch Inflammatory Breast Cancer Research Program, Department of Breast Medical Oncology, MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas, USA)
Alexander A.role: First author of the study showing that the DNA-damage kinase ATM also works in the cytoplasm, where it switches on TSC2 in response to reactive oxygen species and so turns mTORC1 down
Alexander A.sub: Morgan Welch Inflammatory Breast Cancer Research Program, MD Anderson Cancer Center · postdoctoral work in Experimental Radiation Oncology (Khandan Keyomarsi) · Department of Carcinogenesis, MD Anderson, Smithville (Cheryl Walker lab, about 2010)
story: Angela Alexander is first author of ALE2010, done in Cheryl Lyn Walker's group in the Department of Carcinogenesis at MD Anderson's Smithville campus. The paper found that, when reactive oxygen species rise, ATM activates TSC2 in the cytoplasm through the LKB1–AMPK route. This represses mTORC1 and induces autophagy. ATM-deficient cells had high ROS and poorly controlled mTORC1, and rapamycin delayed lymphoma in Atm-deficient mice. The same year she was also an author on a related Autophagy paper on ATM, TSC2 and mTORC1.

She later did postdoctoral work in Khandan Keyomarsi's group in Experimental Radiation Oncology at MD Anderson, moving toward inflammatory breast cancer. Her more recent papers (2022, 2025) list her in the Department of Breast Medical Oncology and the Morgan Welch Inflammatory Breast Cancer Research Program at MD Anderson in Houston. Her exact current title was not found in the sources checked.

highlights.ALE2010: First author: ATM activates TSC2 in the cytoplasm through LKB1 and AMPK in response to ROS, repressing mTORC1 and inducing autophagy.

Walker CL.lab_name: Center for Precision Environmental Health, Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, Texas, USA)
Walker CL.role: Cancer biologist and toxicologist who studies how environmental exposures reprogram the epigenome and target tumour suppressor genes; senior author of the study linking ATM to TSC2 and mTORC1 in the response to oxidative stress
Walker CL.sub: Director, Center for Precision Environmental Health, Baylor College of Medicine · Institute of Biosciences and Technology, Texas A&M (from 2011) · Ruth and Walter Sterling Professor of Carcinogenesis, MD Anderson Cancer Center (2009–2011) · PhD, UT Southwestern (1984) · Member, National Academy of Medicine (2016)
story: Cheryl Lyn Walker is the senior author of ALE2010, done at MD Anderson Cancer Center with Angela Alexander as first author and with collaborators including Kun-Liang Guan, Ken Inoki, Gordon Mills and Michael Kastan. The paper described a cytoplasmic job for ATM: in response to reactive oxygen species, ATM activates the TSC2 tumour suppressor through LKB1 and AMPK, which represses mTORC1 and induces autophagy.

Walker earned a PhD in molecular biology at UT Southwestern (1984) and an MD at Baylor College of Medicine. She held the Ruth and Walter Sterling Professorship of Carcinogenesis at MD Anderson from 2009 to 2011, then directed the Institute of Biosciences and Technology at Texas A&M, and now directs the Center for Precision Environmental Health at Baylor College of Medicine. Her work centres on environmental epigenomics and animal models of gynaecological tumours.

highlights.ALE2010: Senior author: ATM signals to TSC2 in the cytoplasm to repress mTORC1 and induce autophagy when ROS rise.

Sawyers CL.lab_name: Sawyers Lab, Human Oncology & Pathogenesis Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Sawyers CL.role: Physician-scientist known for targeted cancer drugs (ABL inhibitors in leukaemia, antiandrogens in prostate cancer); his UCLA lab helped show that PTEN-deficient tumour cells depend more on mTOR
Sawyers CL.sub: Chair, Human Oncology & Pathogenesis Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering (since 2006) · HHMI Investigator (since 2002) · earlier at UCLA, Jonsson Cancer Center · MD, Johns Hopkins (1985) · Lasker–DeBakey Clinical Award (2009)
story: Charles Sawyers is the senior author of NES2001, done in his lab at UCLA. The study treated isogenic mouse cells and human cancer lines of known PTEN status with the rapamycin analogue CCI-779 (temsirolimus). Cells and tumours lacking PTEN were blocked preferentially, and the drug reversed the extra tumour growth caused by active Akt, placing mTOR downstream of Akt in these models. He is also a co-author of POD2001 from Ramon Parsons' group, a companion paper in the same PNAS issue showing that an mTOR inhibitor reduced neoplasia in Pten+/- mice.

Sawyers studied at Princeton and Johns Hopkins (MD, 1985) and became an HHMI investigator in 2002 while at UCLA. Since 2006 he has chaired the Human Oncology and Pathogenesis Program at Memorial Sloan Kettering. His work contributed to the ABL kinase inhibitors imatinib and dasatinib for chronic myeloid leukaemia, recognised with the 2009 Lasker–DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award, and he co-discovered the antiandrogens enzalutamide and apalutamide for prostate cancer.

highlights.NES2001: Senior author: PTEN-null cells and tumours are preferentially blocked by the mTOR inhibitor CCI-779.
highlights.POD2001: Co-author: an mTOR inhibitor reduces neoplasia and normalises S6 kinase activity in Pten+/- mice.

Podsypanina K.lab_name: Manoury team, Institut Necker Enfants Malades, INSERM U1151 / Université Paris Cité (Paris, France)
Podsypanina K.role: First author of the study showing that an mTOR inhibitor reduced tumour growth and S6 kinase activity in Pten+/- mice; later moved from cancer genetics to tumour immunology
Podsypanina K.sub: Postdoctoral researcher (Inserm), Bénédicte Manoury's team, Institut Necker Enfants Malades, Paris (since 2021) · Institut Curie, Paris · Program in Cancer Biology and Genetics, Memorial Sloan Kettering (Harold Varmus lab, about 2008) · Institute of Cancer Genetics, Columbia University (Ramon Parsons lab, about 1999–2001)
story: Katrina Podsypanina is first author of POD2001, from Ramon Parsons' group at Columbia University. In Pten+/- mice, transformed cells had more phosphorylated Akt and more active p70 S6 kinase. An mTOR inhibitor reduced neoplastic proliferation, tumour size and S6 kinase activity without changing Akt. The paper appeared next to NES2001 from Charles Sawyers' lab, which reached a matching conclusion in cell and xenograft models. She was also first author of a 1999 PNAS paper from the same group describing tumours in multiple organs of Pten-mutant mice.

She then worked in Harold Varmus' lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering, where a 2008 Science paper she led showed that untransformed mouse mammary cells placed in the bloodstream can settle in the lung and later grow into tumours once oncogenes are switched on. After a period at Institut Curie, she joined Bénédicte Manoury's team at the Institut Necker Enfants Malades in Paris in 2021, where she studies TLR9 signalling in dendritic cells and anti-tumour immunity.

highlights.POD2001: First author: an mTOR inhibitor reduces neoplasia and normalises p70 S6 kinase activity in Pten+/- mice.

Parsons R.lab_name: Parsons Lab, Department of Oncological Sciences, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (New York, New York, USA)
Parsons R.role: Cancer geneticist whose Columbia group identified the PTEN tumour suppressor gene in 1997, in parallel with another team; his lab then studied what goes wrong downstream of PTEN loss, including mTOR
Parsons R.sub: Director, Tisch Cancer Institute & Mount Sinai Cancer; Ward-Coleman Professor and Chair of Oncological Sciences, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (since 2013) · Avon Professor of Pathology and Medicine, Columbia University · Postdoc with Bert Vogelstein, Johns Hopkins · MD, PhD, Stony Brook (1992) · Member, National Academy of Medicine (2017)
story: Ramon Parsons is the senior author of POD2001, done at Columbia University with Katrina Podsypanina as first author. In Pten+/- mice, an mTOR inhibitor reduced tumour growth and normalised p70 S6 kinase activity without changing Akt, which pointed to S6K and possibly other mTOR targets as contributors to tumours caused by PTEN loss. It was published in the same PNAS issue as NES2001 from Charles Sawyers' lab, and the two papers reached matching conclusions by different routes.

Parsons studied at Columbia, earned an MD and PhD at Stony Brook (1992) and trained as a postdoc with Bert Vogelstein at Johns Hopkins. At Columbia his group reported PTEN as a gene mutated in brain, breast and prostate cancer (1997). He moved to the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in 2013 as chair of Oncological Sciences and now directs the Tisch Cancer Institute. His lab works on PTEN regulation, PI3K pathway changes in cancer, and breast cancer progression.

highlights.POD2001: Senior author: mTOR inhibition reduces neoplasia and S6 kinase activity in Pten+/- mice without affecting Akt.

Sato T.lab_name: Department of Tumor Control, Aichi Cancer Center Research Institute (Nagoya, Aichi, Japan)
Sato T.role: First author of the study that found single amino-acid changes in mTOR, taken from cancer genome databases, that keep mTOR signalling on during nutrient starvation
Sato T.sub: Senior Researcher, Aichi Cancer Center Research Institute (since 2016) · Assistant Professor, Kitasato University School of Pharmaceutical Sciences (2009–2016) · Postdoctoral fellow, UCLA (2006–2009, Fuyuhiko Tamanoi lab) · PhD, Osaka University Graduate School of Medicine (2006)
story: Tatsuhiro Sato is first author of SAT2010, done as a postdoc in Fuyuhiko Tamanoi's lab at UCLA. The team tested point mutations from cancer genome databases and found two, S2215Y (from a large intestine adenocarcinoma) and R2505P (from a renal cell carcinoma), that kept mTOR signalling active under nutrient starvation. mTORC1 from starved cells carrying the mutants still phosphorylated 4E-BP1, and the cells resisted the shrinkage caused by amino-acid withdrawal. The mutants stayed sensitive to rapamycin. The work grew out of the lab's earlier search for activating TOR mutations in fission yeast, which Sato also co-authored.

Sato earned his PhD at Osaka University in 2006 and was a postdoctoral fellow at UCLA from 2006 to 2009. He was then an assistant professor at the Kitasato University School of Pharmaceutical Sciences and in 2016 moved to the Aichi Cancer Center Research Institute in Nagoya, where he is a senior researcher. His staff page there lists the mTOR pathway as a research theme and his work on mesothelioma.

highlights.SAT2010: First author: the cancer-derived mTOR mutations S2215Y and R2505P keep mTOR signalling on during nutrient starvation.

Tamanoi F.lab_name: Tamanoi Lab, Institute for Integrated Cell-Material Sciences (iCeMS), Kyoto University (Kyoto, Japan)
Tamanoi F.role: Biochemist who studied protein farnesylation and the Rheb–TOR pathway in fission yeast and mammalian cells; senior author of the study that found activating mTOR mutations in human cancer data
Tamanoi F.sub: Program-Specific Professor & PI, iCeMS, Kyoto University · Professor of Microbiology, Immunology & Molecular Genetics, UCLA (from 1997; on faculty since 1993) · University of Chicago (1985–1993) · Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (1980–1985) · Postdoc, Harvard Medical School (1977–1980) · PhD, Nagoya University (1977)
story: Fuyuhiko Tamanoi is the senior author of SAT2010, done in his lab at UCLA with Tatsuhiro Sato as first author. The study showed that two point mutations in mTOR found in cancer genome databases, S2215Y and R2505P, keep mTOR signalling on even when cells are starved of nutrients, while leaving the mutants sensitive to rapamycin. His lab had earlier found activating mutations in the fission yeast TOR kinase Tor2 and in its upstream regulator Rheb, and carried that approach over to mTOR.

Tamanoi trained in biochemistry at Tokyo University and earned his PhD at Nagoya University (1977), followed by postdoctoral work at Harvard Medical School. He was a staff investigator at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory and a faculty member at the University of Chicago before joining UCLA in 1993. His lab identified protein farnesyltransferase and geranylgeranyltransferases and worked on their inhibitors, and later developed mesoporous silica nanoparticles for drug delivery. He now leads a group at the Institute for Integrated Cell-Material Sciences at Kyoto University, working on nanoparticles and cancer therapy.

highlights.SAT2010: Senior author: cancer-derived mTOR point mutations confer constitutive mTOR signalling under nutrient starvation.

Düvel K.lab_name: Research Compliance and Integrity, Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering at Harvard University (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Düvel K.role: First author of the study showing that mTORC1 switches on a metabolic gene program through HIF1α and SREBP, driving glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and lipid synthesis
Düvel K.sub: Director of Research Compliance and Integrity, Wyss Institute at Harvard University (since 2018) · Research Compliance Officer, Harvard FAS and SEAS · Postdoctoral fellow, Manning lab, Harvard School of Public Health (2006–2010) · research on yeast TOR signalling at Princeton University · PhD, Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen
story: Katrin Düvel is first author of DUV2010, done as a postdoctoral fellow in Brendan Manning's lab at the Harvard School of Public Health. Using cells with constitutively active mTORC1 (TSC2 loss) and rapamycin, together with gene expression and metabolite profiling, the team found that mTORC1 activation is enough to drive glycolysis, the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and de novo lipid synthesis. This ran through HIF1α and SREBP1/2 target genes, and SREBP activation needed S6K1.

Before the Manning lab she worked at Princeton University on TOR signalling in budding yeast, including a 2003 Molecular Cell paper on the role of Tap42 in rapamycin-induced changes in gene expression. She earned her PhD at Friedrich-Alexander University in Erlangen. After about 14 years in basic and applied cancer research at Princeton, the Harvard School of Public Health and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, she moved into research administration. Since April 2018 she has been Director of Research Compliance and Integrity at the Wyss Institute at Harvard.

highlights.DUV2010: First author: mTORC1 activates a HIF1α- and SREBP-driven metabolic gene program that supports glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and lipid synthesis.

Bonfils G.lab_name: De Virgilio Lab, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland)
Bonfils G.role: First author of the yeast study proposing that leucyl-tRNA synthetase passes the leucine signal to TORC1 by binding the Rag GTPase Gtr1
Bonfils G.sub: Member of Claudio De Virgilio's group, Department of Biology (Division of Biochemistry), University of Fribourg, Switzerland (about 2009–2012) · current position not confirmed
story: Grégory Bonfils is first author of BON2012, from Claudio De Virgilio's group at the University of Fribourg. In budding yeast, the leucyl-tRNA synthetase Cdc60 bound the Rag GTPase Gtr1 of the EGO complex in a leucine-dependent way, and this contact was reported as necessary and sufficient to pass the leucine signal on to TORC1. When Cdc60 was busy editing wrongly charged tRNA(Leu), the contact was lost. The paper appeared in the same period as Han et al. 2012 in human cells, which also proposed a tRNA synthetase as a leucine sensor upstream of the Rags.

He was also a co-author of the group's 2009 Molecular Cell paper showing that the Vam6 GEF activates Gtr1 and TORC1 in yeast, and of a 2010 commentary on the EGO complex. His later career could not be confirmed from the sources checked here.

highlights.BON2012: First author: in yeast, leucyl-tRNA synthetase binds the Rag GTPase Gtr1 in a leucine-dependent way to control TORC1.

Gulati P.lab_name: Metabolic Research Laboratories, Wellcome-MRC Institute of Metabolic Science, University of Cambridge (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Gulati P.role: First author of the study proposing that amino acids activate mTORC1 through a rise in intracellular calcium and calmodulin binding to hVps34, and later of work linking the obesity gene FTO to amino-acid sensing by mTORC1
Gulati P.sub: University of Cambridge Metabolic Research Laboratories (Giles Yeo and Stephen O'Rahilly groups, about 2013–2017; last confirmed affiliation) · Department of Molecular Oncogenesis, Genome Research Institute, University of Cincinnati (George Thomas and Sara Kozma lab, 2008 paper)
story: Pawan Gulati is first author of GUL2008, done in George Thomas and Sara Kozma's group at the University of Cincinnati. In cultured human cells, adding amino acids raised free intracellular calcium, and this rise was needed for amino acids to switch on mTORC1 and the class III PI3K hVps34. Calcium-bound calmodulin bound a conserved motif in hVps34 that was needed for its lipid kinase activity and for the increase in mTORC1 signalling. The model came before the Rag–Ragulator–GATOR picture and is not part of today's consensus amino-acid pathway.

He then moved to the University of Cambridge Metabolic Research Laboratories, where as first author of a 2013 PNAS paper he reported a role for the obesity-associated gene FTO in coupling amino-acid levels to mTORC1 signalling, and co-authored work on FTO and TMEM18 in appetite and body weight (2015, 2017). His current position could not be confirmed from the sources checked here.

highlights.GUL2008: First author: amino acids raise intracellular calcium, and Ca2+/calmodulin binding to hVps34 is needed for mTORC1 activation in human cells.

Facchinetti V.lab_name: Department of Immunology, MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas, USA)
Facchinetti V.role: First author of the study showing that mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of Akt and conventional PKC as the proteins are made, which helps them fold and stay stable
Facchinetti V.sub: Department of Immunology, MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston (2008; listed again at MD Anderson in 2018) · worked with Bing Su (MD Anderson, then Yale) and Estela Jacinto · current position not confirmed
story: Valeria Facchinetti is first author of FAC2008, written at MD Anderson Cancer Center with Estela Jacinto and Bing Su as senior authors. Cells lacking the mTORC2 components mTOR, SIN1 or rictor lost phosphorylation of Akt and conventional PKC at the turn motif. This phosphorylation did not depend on growth factors and was also found in yeast. It helped newly made Akt and PKC fold and stay stable; without it, Akt was held by Hsp90. mTORC2 controlled the Akt turn-motif and hydrophobic-motif (Ser473) sites independently.

She was also a co-author of two 2010 follow-up papers: one from Su's lab at Yale on Sin1–mTORC2 and Akt2 in B-cell development, and one from Jacinto's lab showing that mTORC2 can sit on ribosomes and phosphorylate the Akt turn motif while the protein is still being made. A 2018 JCI paper on galectin-9 in lupus models again lists her at MD Anderson. Her current position could not be confirmed from the sources checked here.

highlights.FAC2008: First author: mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of Akt and conventional PKC, which controls their folding and stability.

Pende M.lab_name: Cell Growth Control by Nutrients team, Institut Necker Enfants Malades, INSERM (Paris, France)
Pende M.role: Studies how nutrients and growth factors set cell size and metabolism through mTOR and S6 kinase; as a student in George Thomas's lab he helped show that mice lacking S6K1 have small pancreatic beta-cells and low insulin.
Pende M.sub: Team leader, Cell Growth Control by Nutrients, Institut Necker Enfants Malades, Paris · INSERM Directeur de Recherche (since 2007) · INSERM Avenir group leader (2002) · PhD (University of Basel, 2000) and postdoc with George Thomas, Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel · visiting scientist, NICHD/NIH (1993–1996) · pharmacy and pharmacology training, University of Genova
story: Mario Pende was first author of the 2000 Nature study in which mice lacking the kinase S6K1 had low blood insulin and poor glucose tolerance (PEN2000). Their muscle was not insulin resistant; the problem was a smaller pancreatic endocrine mass, explained by beta-cells that were smaller than normal. Two years earlier he was a co-author on the paper that described the small S6K1-knockout mouse and identified a second S6 kinase, S6K2 (SHI1998). Both results come from mice, not people.

Pende trained in pharmacy and pharmacology at the University of Genova and worked at the NICHD in Bethesda before doing his PhD and a short postdoc in George Thomas's lab at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel. He started his own INSERM group in Paris in 2002 and now leads the Cell Growth Control by Nutrients team at the Institut Necker Enfants Malades, which works on mTOR and the Vps15/Vps34 complex and on diseases such as tuberous sclerosis complex.

highlights.PEN2000: First author: S6K1-deficient mice are hypoinsulinaemic and glucose intolerant because their pancreatic beta-cells are smaller.
highlights.SHI1998: Co-author: S6K1-knockout mice are small, and a second S6 kinase, S6K2, partly compensates for the loss.

Meyuhas O.lab_name: Meyuhas Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Faculty of Medicine, Hebrew University of Jerusalem (Jerusalem, Israel)
Meyuhas O.role: Studies how mRNAs with a 5'TOP motif, which encode ribosomal proteins, are controlled, and what phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 does in the cell; his lab built the knock-in mouse in which rpS6 cannot be phosphorylated.
Meyuhas O.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Faculty of Medicine, Hebrew University of Jerusalem (Hebrew University–Hadassah Medical School)
story: Oded Meyuhas was senior author of the 2005 Genes & Development study (RUV2005). His lab made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of ribosomal protein S6 were changed to alanine. Against the model of the time, 5'TOP mRNA translation was unaffected. The mutant cells were smaller, and rapamycin did not shrink them further; adult mice had smaller beta-cells, less pancreatic insulin and poorer glucose tolerance.

Meyuhas is a professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology at the Hebrew University's Faculty of Medicine in Jerusalem. His group has worked for many years on how cells control the production of their own translation machinery through 5'TOP mRNAs.

highlights.RUV2005: Senior author: mice whose rpS6 cannot be phosphorylated keep normal 5'TOP translation but have smaller cells, smaller beta-cells and low insulin.

Jefferies HB.lab_name: Molecular Cell Biology of Autophagy Laboratory (Tooze lab), The Francis Crick Institute (London, England, United Kingdom)
Jefferies HB.role: Biochemist who worked on S6 kinase and 5'TOP mRNA translation in George Thomas's lab and has studied the molecular machinery of autophagy in Sharon Tooze's lab since 2003.
Jefferies HB.sub: Principal Laboratory Research Scientist, Tooze lab, The Francis Crick Institute (since 2003) · Peter Parker's lab, ICRF/Cancer Research UK (2000–2003) · Julian Downward's lab, ICRF (from 1997) · PhD with George Thomas (1994) and postdoc in Basel · BSc in biochemistry, Newcastle University
story: Harold Jefferies was first author of the 1997 EMBO Journal study from George Thomas's lab at the Friedrich Miescher Institute (JEF1997). Using reporter mRNAs and S6 kinase mutants in mammalian cells, the team concluded that rapamycin blocks the translation of 5'TOP mRNAs, which encode ribosomal proteins, by blocking p70 S6 kinase. Later knockout work found 5'TOP control that does not need S6K1, so this step is no longer the accepted model.

Jefferies did his PhD in George Thomas's lab on S6 phosphorylation, S6 kinase and translation, followed by postdoctoral work in Basel. He then moved to London, working on Ras, PI3K and Raf signalling in Julian Downward's lab and on PI3K and PKD drug-discovery projects in Peter Parker's lab, before joining Sharon Tooze's autophagy lab in 2003, now at the Francis Crick Institute.

highlights.JEF1997: First author: rapamycin suppresses 5'TOP mRNA translation in mammalian cells, which the authors traced to inhibition of p70 S6 kinase.

Larsson O.lab_name: Translational Control of Cancer group, Department of Oncology-Pathology, Karolinska Institutet (Stockholm, Sweden)
Larsson O.role: Studies how mRNA translation is altered in cancer and develops methods to measure genome-wide translation; helped show that metformin changes which mRNAs cancer cells translate, through the mTORC1/4E-BP pathway.
Larsson O.sub: Principal Researcher (since 2022) and Head of the Department of Oncology-Pathology (since 2025), Karolinska Institutet · Wallenberg Academy Fellow · Docent (2016) · PhD, Karolinska Institutet (2005)
story: Ola Larsson was first author of the 2012 PNAS study done with the groups of Nahum Sonenberg and Michael Pollak (LAR2012). The team compared genome-wide translation in cancer cells treated with metformin or with the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin and PP242. Metformin changed translation to a similar extent and selectively reduced translation of mRNAs for cell-cycle regulators through the mTORC1/4E-BP pathway. The work was done in cultured cells at in vitro drug concentrations.

Larsson took his PhD at Karolinska Institutet in 2005. He leads the Translational Control of Cancer group in the Department of Oncology-Pathology at Karolinska, which he has headed since 2025. His group studies how altered protein synthesis shapes the proteome of cancer cells and whether it can be targeted.

highlights.LAR2012: First author: metformin reshapes the translatome of cancer cells to an extent comparable to mTOR inhibitors, selectively cutting translation of cell-cycle mRNAs via mTORC1/4E-BP.

Schieke SM.lab_name: Department of Dermatology, Georgetown University Medical Center and MedStar Health (Washington, District of Columbia, USA)
Schieke SM.role: Physician-scientist who, as a postdoc at the NHLBI, helped show that mTOR-raptor activity tracks mitochondrial oxygen consumption in human cells; his lab now studies the metabolism of lymphoid cancers.
Schieke SM.sub: Associate Professor of Dermatology, Georgetown University Medical Center, and attending dermatologist, MedStar Health · formerly Assistant Professor of Dermatology, University of Wisconsin–Madison · dermatology residency, Boston University · postdoctoral fellowship, NHLBI, NIH · MD, Heinrich-Heine-Universität Düsseldorf
story: Stefan Schieke was first author of the 2006 Journal of Biological Chemistry study from Toren Finkel's group at the NHLBI (SCH2006). In cultured human cells, the amount of mTOR-raptor complex correlated with mitochondrial activity, and rapamycin lowered oxygen consumption, membrane potential and ATP-making capacity. mTOR and mTOR-raptor were found in mitochondrial fractions. The link to lifespan was a hypothesis, not tested in this paper.

Schieke trained in medicine in Düsseldorf, spent five years as a postdoctoral fellow at the NHLBI and then completed a dermatology residency at Boston University. After a faculty post at the University of Wisconsin–Madison he moved to Georgetown and MedStar Health in Washington, where he treats patients, including those with cutaneous lymphoma, and studies the metabolic needs of lymphoma and leukaemia cells.

highlights.SCH2006: First author: in human cells the mTOR-raptor complex tracks mitochondrial activity, and rapamycin lowers oxygen consumption and oxidative capacity.

Chan EY.lab_name: Chan Lab, Department of Biomedical and Molecular Sciences, Queen's University (Kingston, Ontario, Canada)
Chan EY.role: Studies how nutrient-sensing kinases, including ULK1, mTORC1 and AMPK, control autophagy and mitochondrial stress responses; in Sharon Tooze's lab he helped identify ULK1 as a kinase needed for starvation-induced autophagy in human cells.
Chan EY.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Biomedical and Molecular Sciences, Queen's University · earlier group leader at the University of Strathclyde, Glasgow · Secretory Pathways Laboratory (Sharon Tooze), Cancer Research UK London Research Institute
story: Edmond Chan was first author of the 2007 Journal of Biological Chemistry study from Sharon Tooze's laboratory at the Cancer Research UK London Research Institute (CHA2007). A kinase-targeted siRNA screen in human HEK293 cells picked out ULK1: knocking it down, but not ULK2, blocked autophagy after amino-acid starvation and after rapamycin, which fits ULK1 acting downstream of mTOR. The team also mapped separate parts of ULK1 needed for its effects and its localisation.

Chan later ran an autophagy lab at the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow, working on ULK1 signalling, AMPK and mTORC1, and the autophagy-lysosome pathway in cancer. His lab is now at Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario, where it studies mitochondria as stress sensors, mitophagy and how cancer cells survive therapy.

highlights.CHA2007: First author: a kinome siRNA screen in human cells identifies ULK1, not ULK2, as required for starvation- and rapamycin-induced autophagy.

Tooze SA.lab_name: Molecular Cell Biology of Autophagy Laboratory, The Francis Crick Institute (London, England, United Kingdom)
Tooze SA.role: Cell biologist who studies how autophagosomes are built in mammalian cells; her lab has identified several mammalian Atg proteins and helped show that ULK1 is needed for starvation-induced autophagy.
Tooze SA.sub: Principal Group Leader, The Francis Crick Institute · group leader at the Imperial Cancer Research Fund / Cancer Research UK London Research Institute (from 1994) · postdoc and staff scientist, EMBL Heidelberg · PhD, EMBL (1986) · EMBO member (2010), FMedSci (2018)
story: Sharon Tooze was senior author of the 2007 Journal of Biological Chemistry study (CHA2007), in which her lab screened human kinases by siRNA and found that ULK1, but not ULK2, was needed for autophagy after amino-acid starvation or rapamycin treatment. The study placed ULK1 downstream of mTOR in human cells, using rapamycin rather than direct measurement of mTORC1 acting on ULK1.

Tooze took her PhD at EMBL in Heidelberg, stayed there as a postdoc and staff scientist, and set up her own lab in London in 1994 at the Imperial Cancer Research Fund, which later became the Cancer Research UK London Research Institute and then part of the Francis Crick Institute. Her early work was on the secretory pathway; from 2006 she turned to autophagy and autophagosome formation.

highlights.CHA2007: Senior author: kinome siRNA screen identifies ULK1 as required for starvation-induced autophagy in human cells.

Russell RC.lab_name: Russell Lab, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of Ottawa (Ottawa, Ontario, Canada)
Russell RC.role: Studies how the nutrient-sensing kinases mTORC1, ULK1 and AMPK control the autophagy machinery; as a postdoc with Kun-Liang Guan he showed that ULK1 phosphorylates Beclin-1 to switch on the autophagy-specific VPS34 complex.
Russell RC.sub: Professor, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of Ottawa (faculty since 2015) · postdoc with Kun-Liang Guan, Department of Pharmacology, UC San Diego · PhD in molecular oncology, University of Toronto · BSc in biochemistry, University of British Columbia
story: Ryan Russell was first author of the 2013 Nature Cell Biology study from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at UC San Diego (RUS2013). After amino-acid withdrawal or mTOR inhibition, ULK1 phosphorylated Beclin-1 at serine 14 and raised the activity of ATG14L-containing VPS34 lipid-kinase complexes. Cells with a non-phosphorylatable Beclin-1 did not increase autophagosomes on starvation, and the matching mutation impaired autophagy in C. elegans embryos.

Russell studied biochemistry at the University of British Columbia and took his PhD in molecular oncology at the University of Toronto, working on oxygen sensing and clear cell renal carcinoma. After his postdoc with Guan he joined the University of Ottawa in 2015, where his lab works on autophagy regulation by nutrient-sensing kinases, signal transduction and metabolism.

highlights.RUS2013: First author: ULK1 phosphorylates Beclin-1 on Ser14 to activate ATG14L-VPS34 complexes after amino-acid starvation or mTOR inhibition.

Sardiello M.lab_name: Sardiello Lab, Division of Genetics and Genomic Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, Missouri, USA)
Sardiello M.role: Geneticist who, in Andrea Ballabio's group, helped show that lysosomal genes share a promoter motif and are switched on together by the transcription factor TFEB; his lab now works on lysosomal storage diseases, especially the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses.
Sardiello M.sub: Professor of Pediatrics, Division of Genetics and Genomic Medicine, Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis · previously Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston · Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Naples
story: Marco Sardiello was first author of the 2009 Science paper from Andrea Ballabio's group at TIGEM in Naples (SAR2009). The team found that most lysosomal genes are expressed in a coordinated way and share a promoter motif (later called the CLEAR element) bound by TFEB. When lysosomes were overloaded, TFEB moved into the nucleus, and extra TFEB increased lysosome numbers and degradation capacity in cultured cells. mTOR was not studied in this paper; later work tied TFEB to mTORC1.

After TIGEM, Sardiello ran a lab in the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston and then moved to Washington University in St. Louis, where he is Professor of Pediatrics. His lab characterises poorly annotated genes linked to inherited disease, with a focus on lysosomal biology and the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses.

highlights.SAR2009: First author: lysosomal genes form a coordinated network with a shared promoter motif regulated by TFEB, which drives lysosome biogenesis.

Peña-Llopis S.lab_name: Translational Genomics group, Department of Ophthalmology, University Hospital Essen (Essen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Peña-Llopis S.role: Cancer geneticist who, in James Brugarolas's lab, found that mTORC1 controls expression of lysosomal V-ATPase genes through TFEB; his group now studies BAP1-mutant uveal melanoma, kidney cancer and cholangiocarcinoma.
Peña-Llopis S.sub: Group Leader, Translational Genomics, Department of Ophthalmology, University Hospital Essen, and member, Center for Medical Biotechnology (ZMB), University of Duisburg-Essen · DKTK partner site Essen · previously Brugarolas lab, UT Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas
story: Samuel Peña-Llopis was first author of the 2011 EMBO Journal study from James Brugarolas's lab at UT Southwestern (PEN2011). Comparing Tsc2-null and wild-type mouse cells with and without rapamycin, the team found genes that follow mTORC1 activity, enriched for subunits of the lysosomal V-ATPase, and showed that a large share of them needed TFEB. In these low-serum conditions active mTORC1 increased nuclear TFEB, the opposite direction to later studies in fed or starved cells.

Peña-Llopis now leads the Translational Genomics group at University Hospital Essen. His group works on cancers with BAP1 mutations, including uveal melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma, and uses patient-derived organoids to test drugs.

highlights.PEN2011: First author: mTORC1 drives expression of lysosomal V-ATPase genes in mouse cells and tissues through the transcription factor TFEB.

Martina JA.lab_name: Puertollano group, Cell and Developmental Biology Center, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Martina JA.role: Cell biologist in Rosa Puertollano's group at the NHLBI who works on how mTORC1 and the Rag GTPases control the lysosomal transcription factors TFEB and TFE3.
Martina JA.sub: Researcher, Rosa Puertollano's group, Cell and Developmental Biology Center (formerly Laboratory of Cell Biology), NHLBI, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda
story: José Martina was first author of the 2013 Journal of Cell Biology study with Rosa Puertollano (MAR2013). In human cells, TFEB reached the lysosome by binding active Rag GTPase heterodimers through its first 30 amino acids, and this recruitment was needed for mTORC1 to phosphorylate TFEB at S211. Depleting the Rags or the Ragulator subunit p18 abolished lysosomal TFEB, and some MITF isoforms behaved the same way.
Martina has worked with Puertollano at the NHLBI for many years on TFEB and TFE3, including a 2025 EMBO Reports study on two TFE3 isoforms that share the same Rag/mTORC1 control.

highlights.MAR2013: First author: active Rag GTPases recruit TFEB and MITF to lysosomes, where mTORC1 phosphorylates and inhibits TFEB.

Yip CK.lab_name: Yip Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and Life Sciences Institute, University of British Columbia (Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada)
Yip CK.role: Structural biologist who uses electron microscopy to study large protein machines; as a postdoc at Harvard Medical School he determined a cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1, and his lab now studies the autophagy machinery.
Yip CK.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of British Columbia · postdoctoral fellow, Harvard Medical School (2006–2010) · PhD (2006) and BSc (2001), University of British Columbia
story: Calvin Yip was first author of the 2010 Molecular Cell study (YIP2010), done in the Department of Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School with Thomas Walz, David Sabatini and Seong Kang. The team purified active human mTORC1 and determined its shape by cryo-EM at about 26 angstrom: an obligate dimer held together by mTOR and Raptor. FKBP12-rapamycin gradually broke the purified complex apart while Torin1 did not, leading the authors to propose that rapamycin blocks S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation by different mechanisms; this disassembly is an in vitro result.

Yip studied at the University of British Columbia, did postdoctoral work at Harvard Medical School and returned to UBC, where he is a professor of biochemistry and molecular biology. His lab studies the structure and biochemistry of the autophagy machinery, chromatin-modifying complexes and rare genetic diseases such as Vici syndrome.

highlights.YIP2010: First author: cryo-EM shows human mTORC1 is a rhomboid dimer, and FKBP12-rapamycin gradually disassembles the purified complex.

Thomas G.MON1999: Senior author: flies lacking S6 kinase are smaller because their cells are smaller, not fewer.
Thomas G.OLD2000: Co-author: the fly TOR homologue dTOR controls growth through dS6K and points to a parallel amino-acid-sensing branch beside insulin signalling.

Thomas G.PEN2000: Senior author: S6K1-deficient mice have small pancreatic beta cells, low insulin and glucose intolerance.
Thomas G.SHI1998: Co-author: S6K1 knockout mice are small, and a second kinase, S6K2, partly takes over S6 phosphorylation.
Thomas G.JEF1997: Senior author: rapamycin suppresses translation of 5'TOP mRNAs through p70 S6 kinase (cells; the S6K step was later revised).

Kozma SC.MON1999: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): Drosophila lacking S6 kinase are small because their cells are smaller.
Kozma SC.GUL2008: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): amino acids activate mTORC1 through calcium-calmodulin signalling to hVps34 (cells).
Kozma SC.PEN2000: Co-author with George Thomas (last author): S6K1-deficient mice have smaller beta cells, low insulin and glucose intolerance.
Kozma SC.SHI1998: Senior author: S6K1 knockout mice are small, and the newly found S6K2 partly compensates for S6 phosphorylation.

Hafen E.MON1999: Showed with George Thomas's group that flies lacking S6 kinase are small because their cells are smaller, not fewer; Hafen was a co-author.

Inoki K.ALE2010: Co-authors a study showing that cytoplasmic ATM signals through LKB1, AMPK and TSC2 to repress mTORC1 when ROS rise.

Shaw RJ.SHAW2004: First author: shows LKB1 is needed to switch off mTOR signalling under low energy through AMPK and TSC2, with raised mTOR signalling in Lkb1 mutant mouse polyps.

Menon S.DUV2010: Co-author: mTORC1 switches on glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and lipid synthesis through HIF1α and SREBP1/2 (cells).

Ballabio A.SET2013: Senior author: TFEB drives its own expression during starvation and controls liver lipid breakdown through PGC-1α and PPARα (mice, worms).
